blocks.md:
The result is typical: the method finds most poisons, and **most is not enough**. 13 surviving poisons (about 1% of the training set) kept the attack working on half the stamped test images, because lesson 12 showed that 12 poisons alone gave 66%. Removing 43 clean 0s cost nothing visible (clean accuracy 0.965), so a more aggressive cut is cheap here; on real data, removing too many rare but genuine examples hurts the very cases you care about.

NIST lists the limits: sanitisation "achieves better results when the poisoning attack controls a relatively large fraction of training data but is not as effective against stealthy poisoning attacks", and Giorgio Severi and colleagues, who studied poisoning of malware classifiers, found spectral signatures and activation clustering "ineffective against clean-label backdoor poisoning on malware classifiers". Trigger reconstruction assumes a fixed trigger pattern, which newer semantic triggers avoid.

Because detection is partial, **provenance** carries much of the weight:

- **Know every source.** Record where each training item came from, when, and its hash at collection time (the split-view defence from the prerequisite course).
- **Version data and models together**, so you can roll back to a known-good pair and retrain.
- **Bill of materials.** An AI bill of materials lists datasets, base models and their versions (ATLAS AML.M0023 AI Bill of Materials).
- **Limit influence by design.** Certified defences such as Deep Partition Aggregation train separate models on disjoint parts of the data and vote, so a few poisons can sway only a few voters.

Backdoor defence is layered: provenance and access control keep poisons out, filtering removes most of what gets in, and retraining from versioned clean data is the fallback. No single detector is a guarantee.

blocks.question: Spectral signatures scored 47 of 60 poisons in the top 90 of 177 images labelled 0. After retraining, attack success was still 0.506. What is the best next step?
options: Declare the model clean, since most poisons were removed
Increase the learning rate
Add adversarial training with PGD
Cut deeper or iterate the filter, and above all fix the data source so poisons cannot enter; then retrain and re-test with the trigger
blocks.explain: A handful of surviving poisons can keep a backdoor alive, as the toy shows. Filtering is a mitigation; closing the data path and retraining from trusted data is the fix. PGD training targets evasion, not backdoors.

blocks.question: Why does spectral filtering look only at examples labelled with the target class?
options: Because poisons carry the target label, and among those examples they form a distinct group that shifts the main direction of variance
Because other classes have no hidden activations
To save memory
Because the trigger is only visible in class 0 images
blocks.explain: BadNets-style poisons are relabelled to the target. Within that label, the trigger gives them a shared representation that differs from clean examples, which the top singular direction picks up.

lessons.title: Membership inference: was this record in the training set?

blocks.md:
Privacy attacks start with the smallest question: was this person's record used to train the model? That alone can be sensitive: if a model was trained only on patients with a condition, membership reveals the condition. Reza Shokri and colleagues (2017) evaluated their attacks on a hospital discharge dataset for exactly that reason. A **membership inference attack** (NISTAML.033; ATLAS AML.T0024.000 Infer Training Data Membership) answers that question from the model's outputs.

Intuition: models are a little more confident, and have lower loss, on examples they were trained on. The more a model **overfits** (fits its training set better than new data), the bigger that gap.

Three generations of attack:

1. **Shadow models** (Shokri et al., 2017): train your own models on data like the target's, where you know who is in and out, and train a classifier to tell members from non-members from the outputs. They attacked models trained by Google's and Amazon's ML-as-a-service offerings.
2. **Loss threshold** (Samuel Yeom and colleagues, 2018): guess "member" when the loss on the true label is below a threshold. They showed "overfitting is sufficient" for membership inference, and also that it is not necessary.
3. **LiRA** (Likelihood Ratio Attack; Carlini et al., posted 2021, published 2022): train many shadow models with and without each example, fit a Gaussian to each case, and ask which explains the target's output better. They argue attacks must be judged by the **true-positive rate at a very low false-positive rate** (for example 0.1%), where average accuracy hides that an attack can be certain about a few people.

blocks.code:
# mia.py: loss-threshold membership inference (Yeom et al. 2018) on our toy
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score
from toy import X, y, tr, te, make, train, acc
mem, non = tr[:100], te[:100]          # 100 members, 100 records never trained on

def attack(m):
    both = torch.cat([mem, non])
    with torch.no_grad():
        loss = F.cross_entropy(m(X[both]), y[both], reduction="none")
    auc = roc_auc_score([1] * 100 + [0] * 100, -loss)   # low loss: guess "member"
    return auc, acc(m, X[mem], y[mem]), acc(m, X[non], y[non])

if __name__ == "__main__":
    for name, kw in {"no regularisation": dict(steps=3000),
                     "weight decay 0.05": dict(steps=3000, wd=0.05)}.items():
        torch.manual_seed(1)
        auc, a_in, a_out = attack(train(make(hidden=256), X[mem], y[mem], **kw))
        print(f"{name:18} train acc {a_in:.2f}  test acc {a_out:.2f}  attack AUC {auc:.3f}")

blocks.md:
**AUC** is the area under the ROC (receiver operating characteristic) curve: the probability that a random member gets a lower loss than a random non-member. 0.5 is a coin flip; 1.0 is perfect. The overfit toy (training accuracy 1.00, test 0.86) gives 0.743. Weight decay, which penalises large weights to reduce overfitting, gives 0.700: better, not solved.

The histogram shows why the attack works and also why it is noisy.

blocks.title: Loss of members and non-members on the overfit toy (counts of 100)

scenes.caption: Members: 80 have loss under 0.001 and all 100 are under 0.01. The model has nearly memorised its training set.
Non-members: spread out, with 23 above 0.1. But 38 also sit under 0.001: easy digits get low loss whether trained on or not.
Threshold 0.01: catches all 100 members (TPR 1.0) but also calls 58 non-members members (FPR 0.58). Many guesses are wrong, which is why LiRA judges at low FPR.

blocks.md:
The attacker's **advantage** is TPR minus FPR (true-positive rate minus false-positive rate) at a chosen threshold: 0.42 at the 0.01 threshold above, and 0.55 at the best threshold for this toy (about 0.003). That number is an average: at 1% FPR the same attack catches only 7 of 100 members. LiRA's insight is that the leak is uneven: unusual **outliers** are memorised much more than typical examples, so a careful attacker can be nearly certain about a few individuals even when the average AUC looks modest. Those individuals are often the ones with the most to lose.

**Defender view.** Prevent: reduce overfitting (regularisation, early stopping, more data); release labels instead of full confidence scores where you can (this raises the attacker's cost but label-only attacks exist); for a guarantee, train with differential privacy (lesson 15). Detect: measure it yourself before release, with a membership inference test on held-out data, including outliers. Respond: if a released model leaks, retrain, and consider retiring the old weights.

"The model is only exposed through an API, so the training data is safe" is false. Query access is all membership inference needs (NIST's capability list). Report TPR at low FPR, not just average accuracy, when you audit.

blocks.question: A model has training accuracy 1.00 and test accuracy 0.86. Which attack does this most directly enable?
options: Backdoor poisoning
Model extraction
Membership inference based on lower loss for training records
Physical-world evasion
blocks.explain: The train-test gap means the model behaves measurably differently on records it saw. Loss-threshold and shadow-model attacks exploit exactly that difference.

blocks.question: Why do Carlini et al. evaluate membership inference by TPR at a low FPR such as 0.1%?
options: Because average accuracy is always 50%
Because it measures whether an attack can identify some members with high confidence, which average metrics hide
Because low FPR makes the attack faster
Because NIST requires it
blocks.explain: An attack with modest average accuracy can still be almost certain for a few outlier records. Privacy harm is about those individuals, so the metric looks at the high-confidence end.

lessons.title: Training with differential privacy: DP-SGD and its price

blocks.md:
Regularisation lowered membership leakage in lesson 14, but by an amount nobody can promise in advance. **Differential privacy** (DP) gives a promise. A training procedure is $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-differentially private if adding or removing any **one** person's record changes the probability of any outcome (any trained model, any prediction) by at most a factor $e^{\varepsilon}$, plus a small slack $\delta$. Small $\varepsilon$ means one record barely matters: the model would have come out almost the same without it. That does not mean nothing can be learned about the person; patterns in the whole population still apply to them.

This lesson covers DP for **training models**. The definition itself, its units and its real-world use (such as the 2020 US Census) are taught in depth in the Privacy engineering course, lesson "Differential privacy: a promise about one person".

blocks.tex: P\left[\mathcal{M}(D) \in S\right] \le e^{\varepsilon}\, P\left[\mathcal{M}(D') \in S\right] + \delta \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \mathrm{TPR} \le e^{\varepsilon}\,\mathrm{FPR} + \delta
blocks.caption: Left: the DP definition for any two datasets D and D' that differ in one record. Right: apply it to the event 'the attack says member' and you get a ceiling on any membership attack's true-positive rate.

blocks.md:
The right-hand side is why DP is the principled defence against membership inference. "The attack says member" is just one possible outcome of looking at the model, so the definition caps it: whatever the attacker does, its true-positive rate is at most $e^{\varepsilon}$ times its false-positive rate, plus $\delta$. NIST AI 100-2 says the same: DP "immediately implies an upper bound on the success" of membership inference, and it protects against data reconstruction too.

Worked numbers with $\delta = 0.001$ and an attacker allowed 1% false positives: at $\varepsilon = 1.4$ the TPR is at most $4.06 \times 0.01 + 0.001 = 0.042$. At $\varepsilon = 10.3$, $e^{10.3}$ is about 30,000 and the formal cap says nothing useful, even if real attacks still do worse.

blocks.title: The DP ceiling on any membership attack

curves.label: DP ceiling: min(1, e^eps x FPR + delta)

scenes.caption: Epsilon 1.4 (the noisiest toy run below): at 1% FPR no attack can exceed about 4% TPR. Confident identification of members is ruled out.
Epsilon 3.3: the ceiling rises quickly, to about 27% TPR at 1% FPR.
Epsilon 10.3: the ceiling hits 1 almost at once, so the proof promises nothing. The real attack may still be weak, but that is luck, not a guarantee.

blocks.md:
**DP-SGD** (differentially private stochastic gradient descent; "stochastic" because each step uses a random sample of the data) is how deep models get this property. Martín Abadi and colleagues (2016) changed ordinary training in three places:

1. **Sample**: each step uses a random subset; here every record joins with probability $q$.
2. **Clip**: compute each example's gradient separately and scale it down to length at most $C$, so no single record can move the model much.
3. **Noise**: add Gaussian noise of size $\sigma C$ to the sum of clipped gradients, then average and step.

A **privacy accountant** adds up the privacy cost of all the steps into one $(\varepsilon, \delta)$. Abadi et al. introduced the moments accountant; libraries such as Opacus, a PyTorch library for training with DP, implement accountants based on Renyi differential privacy (RDP).

blocks.code:
# dpsgd.py: DP-SGD by hand (Abadi et al. 2016)
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F
from torch.func import functional_call, vmap, grad
from opacus.accountants import RDPAccountant
from toy import X, y, make
from mia import attack, mem

def dp_train(sigma, C=1.0, q=0.1, steps=300, lr=2.0):
    torch.manual_seed(1)
    model = make(hidden=256)
    p = {k: v.detach() for k, v in model.named_parameters()}
    loss1 = lambda p, x, t: F.cross_entropy(functional_call(model, p, (x[None],)), t[None])
    acct = RDPAccountant()
    for _ in range(steps):
        b = mem[torch.rand(len(mem)) < q]          # 1) each member joins w.p. q
        g = vmap(grad(loss1), in_dims=(None, 0, 0))(p, X[b], y[b])
        norm = torch.sqrt(sum(v.flatten(1).pow(2).sum(1) for v in g.values()))
        scale = (C / (norm + 1e-6)).clamp(max=1.0)  # 2) clip each to norm <= C
        for k in p:
            s = (g[k] * scale.view(-1, *[1] * (g[k].dim() - 1))).sum(0)
            s = s + sigma * C * torch.randn_like(s)  # 3) Gaussian noise on the sum
            p[k] = p[k] - lr * s / (q * len(mem))    # 4) average and step
        if sigma > 0: acct.step(noise_multiplier=sigma, sample_rate=q)
    model.load_state_dict(p, strict=False)
    return model, acct.get_epsilon(delta=1e-3) if sigma > 0 else float("inf")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    for sigma in (0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0):
        m, eps = dp_train(sigma)
        auc, a_in, a_out = attack(m)
        print(f"noise {sigma:<3} epsilon {eps:6.1f}  train acc {a_in:.2f}  "
              f"test acc {a_out:.2f}  attack AUC {auc:.3f}")

blocks.md:
The toy exaggerates the cost on purpose: 100 records is tiny, and DP noise is fixed while the signal grows with the number of records. With 60,000 MNIST training images Abadi et al. reported 90%, 95% and 97% test accuracy at $\varepsilon$ of 0.5, 2 and 8 ($\delta = 10^{-5}$), and 67%, 70% and 73% on CIFAR-10 at $\varepsilon$ of 2, 4 and 8. DP works best with lots of data per model.

Limits from NIST AI 100-2: DP "does not provide guarantees against model extraction attacks", because it protects the training data, not the model. The analysis is worst-case, so practitioners often use large $\varepsilon$ (the report cites the 2020 US Census at 19.61), and the real privacy is "difficult to estimate". NIST recommends **privacy auditing**: measure leakage empirically, for example by inserting **canaries** (lesson 16) and running membership attacks.

An epsilon without its delta, its unit (one record, one user?) and its accountant is not a privacy claim. Ask what one 'record' means: if a user contributes 500 records, record-level DP says little about that user.

**Defender view.** Prevent: for models trained on sensitive personal data, plan for DP-SGD from the start (budget, data volume, accountant) rather than bolting it on; combine it with data minimisation. Detect: audit every release with a membership attack and canaries, and track the measured leakage like any other regression metric. Respond: if an audit shows leakage beyond what the claim allows, treat the model as a data exposure: retrain, and check whether removal of individuals' data is required (the Machine unlearning course covers removing data from trained models).

blocks.question: DP-SGD clips each example's gradient to norm C before adding noise. Why clip per example rather than the averaged gradient?
options: Clipping per example bounds how much any one record can move the model, which is what lets the noise hide that record
It speeds up training
It prevents adversarial examples
Clipping the average is not possible in PyTorch
blocks.explain: The privacy proof needs a bound on each record's influence (its sensitivity). Clipping the average would let one extreme record dominate before clipping.

blocks.question: A vendor says its model is 'trained with differential privacy, epsilon 50'. What is the most accurate reading?
options: Very strong privacy: 50 is a large safety margin
Epsilon only matters for model extraction
It means 50 records were removed
The formal guarantee is weak: e^50 is astronomically large, so the bound on attacks is meaningless; ask for an empirical audit
blocks.explain: Larger epsilon means weaker privacy. At 50 the multiplicative bound says nothing, so only empirical auditing tells you how much actually leaks.

blocks.md:
Membership inference asks a yes-or-no question about a record you already have. The stronger attacks recover the data itself. NIST calls this **reconstruction** (NISTAML.032) for predictive models and **data extraction** for generative ones; ATLAS has AML.T0024.001 Invert AI Model.

**Model inversion.** Matt Fredrikson, Somesh Jha and Thomas Ristenpart (2015) attacked face-recognition models that return confidence scores. Given only a person's name (the class label) and query access, they searched for the input that maximises that person's confidence, recovering a recognisable image. Workers on Amazon's Mechanical Turk (a paid crowd-work site), shown the reconstruction, could pick the right person out of a line-up: the skilled ones with close to 95% accuracy for the simplest (softmax) model, and all workers above 80% on average. The same paper estimated whether survey respondents had admitted to cheating on their partner, from a lifestyle-survey model, a form of **attribute inference** (inferring a sensitive field of a training record).

Their countermeasures are still the basic ones: **rounding reported confidence values** "can drastically reduce the effectiveness" of the attacks, and so can training choices that limit how much sensitive features drive the model. The authors were careful to add that they had not checked whether attacks could adapt to those countermeasures.

**Generative models memorise.** The prerequisite course showed that GPT-2 could be made to emit hundreds of verbatim training sequences (Carlini et al., 2020), including some that appeared in only one document. Later work found the same in other model families:

- **Diffusion models** (image generators such as Stable Diffusion): Carlini et al. (2023) extracted "over a thousand training examples", from photos of individual people to trademarked logos.
- **Aligned chat models**: Milad Nasr, Carlini and colleagues (2023) attacked ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo).

**Case: extracting ChatGPT's training data, 2023.** Nasr et al. found that prompting gpt-3.5-turbo to repeat a single word many times made it eventually **diverge** from chat behaviour and emit long passages of memorised text, at a rate they put at 150 times higher than normal. With about USD 200 of API queries they extracted over 10,000 unique verbatim training examples, confirmed by matching against a 9 TB auxiliary collection of public web text; the longest was over 4,000 characters. They found the flaw on 11 July 2023, disclosed it to OpenAI on 30 August, and waited 90 days before publishing. Their conclusion for defenders: "current alignment techniques do not eliminate memorization".

How do you measure memorisation in your own model before someone else does? Carlini and colleagues' **Secret Sharer** method (2018) plants **canaries**: random secret-like strings such as "the pin is 72913", inserted into the training data a known number of times. After training, rank the real canary against every other possible value by how likely the model finds each. The **exposure** is $\log_2$ of the number of candidates minus $\log_2$ of the canary's rank. With 100,000 possible PINs the maximum is $\log_2 100{,}000 = 16.6$ bits, meaning the model ranks the secret first. Google used this method to limit exposure in Smart Compose, its email autocompletion model.

blocks.code:
# canary.py: measure memorisation with a planted canary (Carlini et al. 2018)
import math, random
from collections import Counter
random.seed(0)
K = 4                                         # character 4-gram language model
CANARY = "the pin is 72913"

def fit(lines):
    grams, ctx = Counter(), Counter()
    for s in lines:
        s = "^" * (K - 1) + s
        for i in range(K - 1, len(s)):
            grams[s[i - K + 1:i + 1]] += 1; ctx[s[i - K + 1:i]] += 1
    return grams, ctx

def logp(model, s):                           # log2 P(s), add-0.1 smoothing
    grams, ctx = model; s = "^" * (K - 1) + s
    return sum(math.log2((grams[s[i-K+1:i+1]] + 0.1) / (ctx[s[i-K+1:i]] + 1.0))
               for i in range(K - 1, len(s)))

background = [f"the pin is {random.randrange(10**5):05d}" for _ in range(5000)]
for repeats in (0, 1, 2, 4, 16):
    model = fit(background + [CANARY] * repeats)
    scores = [logp(model, f"the pin is {c:05d}") for c in range(10**5)]
    mine = logp(model, CANARY)
    rank = 1 + sum(sc > mine for sc in scores)   # 1 = most likely of all 100,000
    print(f"inserted {repeats:2}x  rank {rank:6}  exposure {math.log2(10**5 / rank):5.1f} bits")

blocks.title: Exposure of a planted secret versus copies in the training data

scenes.caption: Not inserted: the canary ranks 70,000th of 100,000. Exposure 0.5 bits: the model knows nothing about it.
One copy: rank 14,164, exposure 2.8 bits. Two copies: rank 1,190, 6.4 bits. Each repetition makes the secret stand out more.
Four copies: rank 2, 15.6 bits; sixteen: rank 1, the full 16.6 bits. An attacker trying the model's top guesses gets the PIN almost at once.

blocks.md:
The toy reproduces the main empirical finding at small scale: **repetition drives memorisation**. [Nikhil Kandpal, Eric Wallace and Colin Raffel (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.06539) measured it in language models: a sequence present 10 times in the training data is generated "~1000 times more often" than one present once, and after **deduplicating** training data, models became "considerably more secure" against these attacks. Web-scale data is full of duplicates, from boilerplate to leaked records copied across many sites.

**Defender view.** Prevent: remove secrets and personal data before training, deduplicate, and use DP-SGD where records are sensitive. Detect: put canary tests in your training pipeline and fail the run if exposure exceeds a threshold; for deployed generators, compare outputs against a sample of training data for long verbatim matches; watch for odd prompting patterns at volume, such as heavy repetition. Respond: block the pattern, then fix the data and retrain, because filters on output do not remove memorised data.

A model trained on secrets can repeat them to anyone who can query it. Repetition in the training data is the biggest single factor, so deduplication and scrubbing come first, measurement with canaries second, and DP when records are sensitive.

blocks.question: A canary inserted 4 times reaches exposure 15.6 bits out of a possible 16.6. What does that mean in practice?
options: The canary was not memorised
The model ranks the secret second among 100,000 candidates, so an attacker who tries its top guesses finds it almost at once
The model can generate 15.6 copies
Exposure only applies to images
blocks.explain: Exposure is log2(candidates) - log2(rank). 16.6 - 15.6 = 1 bit means rank 2. High exposure means extraction by guessing in order of likelihood is cheap.

blocks.question: Which preprocessing step most directly reduces training-data extraction according to Kandpal et al.?
options: Adding more parameters
Lowering the learning rate
Deduplicating the training data
Translating the data into another language
blocks.explain: Regeneration grows superlinearly with how often a sequence appears. Removing duplicates removes most of the easily extracted material.

lessons.title: Model extraction: stealing a model through its API

blocks.md:
**Model extraction** (NISTAML.031; ATLAS AML.T0024.002 Extract AI Model) copies a model's behaviour or parameters through its prediction interface. Motives: avoid paying per query, steal a competitor's work, or get a white-box copy to craft evasion attacks offline (lesson 5). The prerequisite course listed it under OWASP's LLM10 Unbounded Consumption; here is how it works.

Tiny example: a logistic regression returns $p = \sigma(w^\top x + b)$. Take the **logit** (log-odds) of the returned probability, $\ln(p/(1-p))$, and you get $w^\top x + b$ exactly: one linear equation in the unknown weights per query.

Florian Tramer and colleagues (2016) built on that. With $d$ features, $d + 1$ queries give $d + 1$ equations, enough to solve for all weights and the bias: **equation-solving extraction**. They extended it to multiclass models and neural networks and used other techniques for decision trees. Against Amazon Machine Learning they extracted a logistic regression on a digits dataset, a 100% equivalent model, with 650 queries in about 70 seconds; BigML's (another ML-as-a-service provider) decision trees took 1,150 to 4,013 queries. Even when confidence values were omitted, extraction "still admits potentially harmful model extraction attacks", needing up to 100 times more queries.

blocks.code:
# extract.py: equation-solving extraction (Tramer et al. 2016) of OUR OWN model
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
X, y = load_digits(return_X_y=True); X = X / 16
secret = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000).fit(X, y == 3)   # "is it a 3?"

def api(q, decimals=None):                 # what a prediction API returns
    p = secret.predict_proba(q)[:, 1]
    return p if decimals is None else np.round(p, decimals)

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
def steal(n_queries, decimals=None):
    Q = rng.uniform(0, 1, (n_queries, 64))
    p = api(Q, decimals)
    ok = (p > 0) & (p < 1)                 # a rounded 0 or 1 says almost nothing
    Q, p = Q[ok], p[ok]
    logit = np.log(p / (1 - p))            # = w . x + b, a LINEAR equation
    A = np.hstack([Q, np.ones((len(Q), 1))])
    wb, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(A, logit, rcond=None)
    return wb

true = np.append(secret.coef_[0], secret.intercept_[0])
for n, d in [(65, None), (65, 2), (650, 2), (6500, 2)]:
    wb = steal(n, d)
    agree = np.mean(((X @ wb[:64] + wb[64]) > 0) == secret.predict(X))
    print(f"{n:5} queries, decimals={d}: max weight error {np.abs(wb - true).max():.2e}, "
          f"agreement {agree:.3f}")

blocks.md: **Case: stealing part of production LLMs, 2024.** Carlini and colleagues (Google DeepMind, ETH Zurich and others) showed that LLM APIs which return log-probabilities and accept a **logit bias** (a parameter that adds a chosen amount to chosen tokens' scores) leak the model's final layer. The final layer maps a hidden vector of size $h$ to scores for every token, so all output score vectors lie in an $h$-dimensional subspace; enough queries reveal $h$ and the layer itself, up to symmetries. For under USD 20 they extracted the entire projection matrix of OpenAI's Ada and Babbage models, confirming hidden sizes of 1,024 and 2,048, and they recovered the hidden size of gpt-3.5-turbo. They had OpenAI's approval before extracting parameters, and after disclosure OpenAI and Google changed their APIs to make the attack harder.

**Case: distillation campaigns against Claude, 2026.** Extraction also works at the level of behaviour. **Distillation** means training a model on another model's outputs; it is a normal technique when a lab distils its own models. In February 2026 [Anthropic reported](https://www.anthropic.com/news/detecting-and-preventing-distillation-attacks) that three AI labs, DeepSeek, Moonshot and MiniMax, had generated over 16 million exchanges with Claude through about 24,000 fraudulent accounts, using proxy services, to train their own models on Claude's capabilities in agentic reasoning, tool use and coding. Anthropic said what gave the campaigns away was the pattern, "Massive volume concentrated in a few areas, highly repetitive structures", and described its response: classifiers and behavioural fingerprinting of API traffic, intelligence sharing, stronger account verification, and countermeasures that make outputs less useful for illicit distillation. ATLAS: AML.CS0056. In October 2026 Anthropic reported early evidence that newer defences cut distillers' harvested data by 90 to 99%.

**Defender view.** Prevent: return the least information the product needs (labels or rounded scores; no full log-probabilities unless needed; ATLAS AML.M0002), rate-limit and price per query (AML.M0004), and verify accounts where abuse is cheap. Detect: per-account query analytics: volume, coverage of the input space, synthetic or random-looking inputs, repetitive templates spread across linked accounts. Respond: suspend clusters of accounts together, share indicators with peers, and assume a stolen copy can now be used for white-box evasion. NIST's caveat applies: these measures "can be circumvented by motivated and well-resourced attackers", and differential privacy does not help here at all, since it protects the data, not the model.

Every answer an API gives is information about the model. Precision (full scores, logprobs) makes extraction cheap; volume makes any extraction possible. Control both, and watch accounts in aggregate, because large campaigns spread across many of them.

blocks.md:
Findings are only useful if others can act on them. Two vocabularies make that possible: **NIST AI 100-2** classifies the attack (stage, goal, capability), and **MITRE ATLAS** describes what the attacker did, step by step, in the style of ATT&CK: 16 tactics, from Reconnaissance and AI Model Access through AI Attack Staging to Exfiltration and Impact, with techniques under each, mitigations, and real case studies.

ATLAS is maintained as data as well as a website, so you can check ids against a named release instead of trusting memory. This course uses ATLAS data v5.6.0, the last release of the single-file ATLAS.yaml, which the repository now marks as deprecated. Monthly releases since then (for example v2026.10) use a new format and rename or move some entries: membership inference is now AML.T0137.000, model inversion AML.T0137.002, Create Proxy AI Model is now Replicate AI Model Behavior, and Extract AI Model (AML.T0024.002) is gone, covered by Replicate Behavior from Model Outputs (AML.T0005.001). Always cite the release you checked.

blocks.md:
**A test plan for a model you own.** Before release, run and record:

1. **Threat model**: who can query, who can write training data, which inputs an attacker controls, and the realistic size of their changes.
2. **Evasion**: PGD or AutoAttack at that budget, plus an adaptive attack for any defence, plus the lesson 9 sanity checks. Report clean and robust accuracy.
3. **Poisoning and backdoors**: list every write path into training data; run a spectral or activation-clustering scan on the final training set; verify the provenance of pre-trained weights.
4. **Privacy**: a membership attack (report TPR at low FPR), canary exposure for generative models, and the DP budget if one is claimed.
5. **Extraction**: what the API returns, its rate limits, and the query analytics you will watch.

Keep the practitioner view from lesson 6 in mind. Apruzzese et al.'s survey of real incidents concluded that actual attackers mostly use simple tactics, and that defences should start from "precise and cost-driven threat modeling". So prioritise in this order: controls that are cheap and broad (provenance, access control, rate limits, ensembles of diverse signals, monitoring), then measured robustness for the specific threats that matter, then certificates where a guarantee is worth the cost.

The prerequisite course's LLM application risks (prompt injection, excessive agency, improper output handling) sit on top of everything here. A model can be robust, private and unpoisoned and still be talked into misusing its tools; those risks are handled at the application layer as that course showed.

**Practise legally.** Every lab in this course runs on models you train yourself, which is where adversarial ML practice belongs:

- Re-run the labs with a different dataset or model size, and try to break your own defences with an adaptive attack before you trust them.
- [RobustBench](https://robustbench.github.io/): leaderboards and a model zoo of published robust models to evaluate locally with standard attacks.
- [MITRE ATLAS](https://atlas.mitre.org/) and its [data repository](https://github.com/mitre-atlas/atlas-data): read the case studies used in this course (AML.CS0003, CS0009, CS0032, CS0056) end to end.
- [Opacus](https://opacus.ai/): tutorials for training your own models with DP-SGD.
- [CyLab Security Academy](https://cylabacademy.org/): Carnegie Mellon's free capture-the-flag practice for general security skills.

Never point these techniques at a model or API you do not own without written permission: query-based attacks against a provider's service break its terms and, depending on the jurisdiction, computer misuse law.

Name the attack (NIST), describe the steps (ATLAS), measure it on your own model with honest attacks, and assign the mitigation to an owner. Cheap, broad controls first; measured robustness and privacy guarantees where the threat justifies their cost.
